messages.body_plain:
greetings,

i have a couple questions i'm hoping someone can help with. i am working specifically with a large bipartite network (men/women), but i believe the questions are generally relevant. i am interested in including a number of effects in my models that aren't currently included in ergm-terms. i know there is a way for me to code up these terms myself (using the ergmuserterms package)- but for those of us whose programming knowledge is basic/non-existent, i'm wondering if other workarounds are available. specifically, i'm interested in the following two scenarios:

currently, there are terms available for homophily on a certain attribute (nodematch), and one can even break this down by the value of the attribute using diff=TRUE. so in my network, i can see if college-educated people tend to contact one another. instead, i want to know if the tendency towards educational homophily varies by gender- in other words, i want to see if the tendency for college-educated men to contact college-educated women is different from the tendency of college-educated women to contact college educated men. rather than coding a term for this effect, i wonder if instead i could just create an edge covariate (i.e. a new network X) in which, say, every possible tie from a college-educated male to a college-educated female is present. then, if i include two terms in the model- nodematch(collegeeducation) and edgecov(X)- the former term will essentially indicate educational homophily from women to men, while the latter will indicate educational homophily from men to women. is this accurate? (the same reasoning could therefore be extended to any number of scenarios, in which we expect homophily on covariate A to vary by covariate B.)

my second question is similar, but instead involves reciprocity (i appreciate the addition of the new "by" argument, by the way!). one example is that i want to know whether women are more likely to reciprocate ties to men with a similar income. let's say my network is called "network," and i have an edge covariate called "absdiffincome" indicating the absolute difference in income between every possible dyad. to find the answer to my question, my thought is that i could 1) begin with network, and drop all ties from women to men (i.e. keep only ties from men to women); 2) take the transpose of this network; and 3) code this transpose network with values from absdiffincome (i.e. cell-wise multiply the values of [transpose network] with the values of [absdiffincome]), and use this final network as a new edge covariate. am i totally off my rocker here, or would this actually produce the type of effect i am looking for? and if all of this happens to work as i think it might, are there any drawbacks to doing things this way other than the extra hassle?

many thanks, and apologies for the lengthy explanation!

-kevin

Kevin Lewis

re: the second part, i apologize for the ambiguity- i think i was also jumping the gun a little bit. my original interest is indeed in whether men are more likely to reciprocate ties than women. i initially also figured that the "by" option would take care of this- but then realized that, because my network is bipartite, counting every mutual tie involving a female is identical to counting every mutual tie (because all mutual ties by definition involve a male and a female), and so the mutual term with the "by" option for women is identical to the generic mutual term by itself.

i see what you are saying about dyads either being reciprocal or not- but it seems to me that (even with cross-sectional data) one should be able to get at this difference- in a sense by comparing how many male --> female ties are returned with how many female --> male ties are returned. if virtually all of the asymmetric ties in a network are male --> female, for instance- and there are virtually no asymmetric female --> male ties- wouldn't this suggest that men are more likely to respond to women than women are to men? thus, i was trying to get at this with the transpose/edge covariate effect (we can ignore the additional income complication for the moment).

as it turns out, however, i DO have a timestamp for each tie- and so the network i'm using is actually a collapsed longitudinal network. given this information, i would love to hear any thoughts you might have on how to go about using this in order to disentangle the type of gender*reciprocity interaction i hope to get at :).

(happy to also take this offline, unless you think the list would benefit.)

thanks again!!!

-kevin

p.s. please forgive my complicated initial posing of the question in terms of the income question- it seems as though if we are able to get a solution to the basic male vs. female reciprocity issue above, then i would probably be able to extend this to define additional interaction effects between gender, reciprocity, and dyadic covariates.

Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does ergm
(the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of pique,
but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the types of
questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in seeing other
papers that expand on such an approach.

modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a complicating rather
than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the network as unipartite
with attributes (wholly apart from the heteronormative implications). I
trust there is an underlying statistical rationale, but perhaps someone
could hold my hand and elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be
superior to a unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
female-female interactions?

Thanks and apologies for hijacking the thread in advance...

Brian

> types of questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in

Thanks, Brian. Indeed you're not demonstrating your ignorance of the 
package - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was 
answering Kevin's question more from the perspective of the sort of 
model that would in theory make sense given the question he was trying 
to answer, rather than what ergm would actually do. A quick double-check 
of ergm, via the following code:

a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
b[,]

indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are 
simultaneously bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the 
network package does, however).

> Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me
> that modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a
> complicating rather than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the
> network as unipartite with attributes (wholly apart from the
> heteronormative implications). I trust there is an underlying
> statistical rationale, but perhaps someone could hold my hand and
> elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be superior to a
> unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
> female-female interactions?

My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which 
there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the 
real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by 
definition be between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest 
to model it as bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes 
those classes of nodes, as long as there is a cross-class requirement of 
some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class 
parameters fixed at -Inf (which is what happens if you send in a network 
with no ties across classes for estimation) is statistically equivalent, 
so from a practical standpoint I really don't think it matters.  To me 
it just seems cleaner.

I'm not sure what domain of data Kevin was modeling, and whether the 
requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the 
phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case 
could be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable 
to model it as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically 
reasonable to model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the 
distinction between the two is probably pretty fuzzy.

And, in this case, since ergm doesn't handle bipartite directed 
networks, it sounds like Kevin is going to have to go the route you 
suggest regardless of philosophical preferences!

I'd love to hear others' thoughts on this.

Steve

i believe the model is doing what it's supposed to be doing. when i run a model solely with the edges term, the parameter estimate it gives me is identical to what i would expect if the network was being modeled as bipartite- in other words, the parameter estimate corresponds to the density of a BIPARTITE network (where only a subset of dyads are eligible), not a one-mode network (where all dyads are eligible). to confirm this, i took the exact same network, but converted it into a one-mode network instead- and indeed, when i do this and model the new network, the parameter estimate for "edges" changes and now corresponds to the density of my network when all dyads are considered.

also, i don't see why one-mode terms shouldn't apply to two-mode data. in my network below, the attribute "female" happens to be identical to the partitioning of the network into two modes (according to gender). therefore, this term still tells me that women are more likely to receive ties than men- which, in this case, is identical to saying men send more ties than women.

all this is to say, i believe ergm is indeed modeling my directed, bipartite network, and doing so correctly. which is good news, right? :)

-kevin

package - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was
answering Kevin's question more from the perspective of the sort of
model that would in theory make sense given the question he was trying
to answer, rather than what ergm would actually do. A quick double-check
of ergm, via the following code:

a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
b[,]

indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are
simultaneously bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the
network package does, however).

> Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me

My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which
there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the
real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by
definition be between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest
to model it as bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes
those classes of nodes, as long as there is a cross-class requirement of
some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class
parameters fixed at -Inf (which is what happens if you send in a network
with no ties across classes for estimation) is statistically equivalent,
so from a practical standpoint I really don't think it matters.  To me
it just seems cleaner.

I'm not sure what domain of data Kevin was modeling, and whether the
requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the
phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case
could be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable
to model it as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically
reasonable to model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the
distinction between the two is probably pretty fuzzy.

And, in this case, since ergm doesn't handle bipartite directed
networks, it sounds like Kevin is going to have to go the route you
suggest regardless of philosophical preferences!

I'd love to hear others' thoughts on this.

Steve

Kevin's comment about the relative eligibility of ties is an important
distinction I missed when thinking through the 1vs2 mode approaches.

Regarding the applicability of terms, I'm going off of pages 15 and 16 of
the Sunbelt statnet tutorial which implies that nodeifactor shouldn't apply
to bipartite networks:

http://csde.washington.edu/statnet/Resources/Sunbelt2011/ergm%20tutorial%20sunbelt%202011.pdf

To return to the distinction, I wonder if the nodeifactor is thus
calculating conditioned on all nodes (so that male-male, female-female,
male-female, female-male ties are all considered) rather than just
male-female, female-male nodes which "bipartite edges" appropriately does.

> i believe the model is doing what it?s supposed to be doing. when i run a
> model solely with the edges term, the parameter estimate it gives me is
> identical to what i would expect if the network was being modeled as
> bipartite- in other words, the parameter estimate corresponds to the density
> of a BIPARTITE network (where only a subset of dyads are eligible), not a
> one-mode network (where all dyads are eligible). to confirm this, i took the
> exact same network, but converted it into a one-mode network instead- and
> indeed, when i do this and model the new network, the parameter estimate for
> ?edges? changes and now corresponds to the density of my network when all
> dyads are considered.****
>
> ** **
>
> also, i don?t see why one-mode terms shouldn?t apply to two-mode data. in
> my network below, the attribute ?female? happens to be identical to the
> partitioning of the network into two modes (according to gender). therefore,
> this term still tells me that women are more likely to receive ties than
> men- which, in this case, is identical to saying men send more ties than
> women.****
>
> ** **
>
> all this is to say, i believe ergm is indeed modeling my directed,

I think that bipartite graphs were used originally to model 2-mode 
networks.  In that case, there really is no possibility of a link 
between the nodes within mode.

In this case, it's an empirical question, but it sounds like Kevin's data 
collection ensured that there are no withn-group ties.  If so, this is a 
bipartite (directed) network.

Hi all,

So, indeed, ergm should *not* currently be used with networks that are 
both bipartite and directed.  This should be consistent with all of the 
documentation out there; if anyone knows of documentation that we've 
produced that says (or even suggests) otherwise, please point us to it 
so we can correct it.

The reason this is, is that the MCMC estimation code treats all 
bipartite networks as undirected, and only proposes toggles Yij where i 
and j are of different bipartite classes (i.e. of different modes of a 
two-mode network), and i<j. It is the last criterion that makes it work 
for undirected networks, but not for directed.

Some of the confusion arises from the fact that we put in error messages 
to block users from using ergm terms with directed bipartite networks 
for some terms and not others.  Specifically, for those terms that are 
specific to bipartite networks (e.g. b1degree), we put in checks for 
both bipartiteness and for directedness.  However, for those terms that 
are not bipartite-specific (nodeifactor), we didn't do a double-check 
and block those fitting both criteria. Kevin appears to have only used 
terms in the latter category, so didn't get an error.

We will add errors to all terms to make sure they prevent use on 
directed bipartite networks in the next update of ergm.

Note again that the network package can handle with directed bipartite 
networks. This limitation is specific to ergm, given the complexities of 
the MCMC estimation code.

I imagine some of you are wondering if we plan to add capabilities to 
ergm for directed bipartite networks in the future.  As far as I know it 
hasn't been on the (already long) list of things to do (but other 
statnet developers, correct me if I'm wrong on that).  However, a large 
show of hands from those who are interested in such capability could 
help prioritize it.  If you're in that camp, feel free to email me and 
let me know (no need to copy the entire listserv).

Thanks for bringing this up, Kevin, and thanks to Brian for helping to 
clarify.

Steve
(+statnet team)

messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

Let me elucidate one point. I know that the longest path problem is
NP-complete, but I was wondering whether there exist any approximate
optimization techniques (like, for instance, on modularity
maximization for community detection, which is also NP-complete).

In any case, I should say that part of my problem is not so general
and perhaps you may be able to suggest to me another idea to deal with
it. As a matter of fact, I am interested in determining pairs of
vertices (let's say in a simple undirected graph) which are joined
together by (possibly multiple) paths having the same length (and
finding this unique path length for each pair of such vertices). In
other words, this is the case when geodesic paths are also maximal
length paths. Notice that I'd also like to include the degenerate case
of closed paths (of length larger or equal to three) between a vertex
and itself, i.e., cycles passing from a vertex. In this particular
case, I'm interested in determining vertices from which at most one
cycle might pass (and the period of these cycles).

My motivation for this computation is to be able to formulate problems
of transitivity (local clustering, small-worldedness, structural holes
etc.) in a more formal way (graph-theoretically) than in the existing
approaches.

Any clues?

Best,

--Moses

messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to label the edges in a network plot automatically?
I'm trying to create some demo plots of how 2-mode networks can be
transformed into two 1-mode networks, and scaling the width of the
edge doesn't really demonstrate the value of the edge sufficiently.

Thanks,
Sam

Sample Code:

#producing figure 2: example of a two-mode network and the resulting
1-mode networks
ex = matrix(c(
  0,1,1,0,
  1,1,1,0,
  0,0,1,1,
  1,0,0,1,
  1,1,0,0
  ),nrow=5,byrow=T)
row.names(ex) <- paste("U",1:5,sep='')
colnames(ex) <- paste("T",1:4,sep='')
ex1 = t(ex)%*%ex
diag(ex1)=0
row.names(ex1) <- colnames(ex1) <- colnames(ex)
ex2 = ex%*%t(ex)
diag(ex2)=0
row.names(ex2) <- colnames(ex2) <- row.names(ex)

exNet = network(as.sociomatrix(ex))

exNet2 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex2))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

I don't know if it is possible to label edges, but I have found a 
combination of edge width and edge color to be acceptable. Try the 
following modification of your code. You can replace k=0.5 and ^3 by 
other values to tweak the result.

Take care

Philip

ex = matrix(c(
   0,1,1,0,
   1,1,1,0,
   0,0,1,1,
   1,0,0,1,
   1,1,0,0
   ),nrow=5,byrow=T)
row.names(ex) <- paste("U",1:5,sep='')
colnames(ex) <- paste("T",1:4,sep='')
ex1 = t(ex)%*%ex
diag(ex1)=0
row.names(ex1) <- colnames(ex1) <- colnames(ex)
ex2 = ex%*%t(ex)
diag(ex2)=0
row.names(ex2) <- colnames(ex2) <- row.names(ex)

exNet = network(as.sociomatrix(ex))
exNet1 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex1))
set.edge.value(exNet1,'number',ex1)
exNet2 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex2))
set.edge.value(exNet2,'number',ex2)

assign.edge.color <- function(x, k=4) {
   colors <- character(length(x))
   mx <- max(x)
   mn <- min(x)
   for (i in 1:length(x)) {
     colors[i] <- gray((1 - (x[i] / mx))^k)
   }
   return(colors)
}

par(mfrow=c(2,2),mar=c(1,1,1,1))
plot(exNet,vertex.col=c(rep(2,5),rep(3,4)),main='Sample 2-mode 
network',vertex.cex=3,displaylabels=TRUE)
